Mark 1.summary: Mark begins with John the Baptist preaching repentance and baptizing in the wilderness, preparing the way for the stronger one to come (Mark 1:1–8). Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends, and a heavenly voice calls him the beloved Son; the Spirit drives him into the wilderness for forty days of testing (Mark 1:9–13). After John's arrest, Jesus announces God's approaching kingdom and calls Simon, Andrew, James, and John (Mark 1:14–20). In Capernaum he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, prays alone, and travels to preach elsewhere. He cleanses a man with a skin disease and instructs him to follow the prescribed priestly procedure, but the spreading report makes public entry into towns difficult (Mark 1:21–45). The opening presents Jesus' identity, authority, mission, and growing public attention.
Mark 1.whereWeAre: Within the biblical narrative, Mark begins with John the Baptist preaching repentance and baptizing in the wilderness, preparing the way for the stronger one to come (1:1–8). Independently, first-century Judea and Galilee were under Roman imperial influence, with varied Jewish movements and practices. Individual speeches and miracles are known chiefly from the Gospel accounts. This setting helps clarify the pressures, audiences and imagery of Mark 1. The events and words above are reported by Mark; details without independent corroboration should not be treated as independently documented historical facts.

Mark 2.summary: Jesus returns to Capernaum, where four men lower a paralyzed man through a roof. He first declares the man's sins forgiven, provoking scribes to accuse him of blasphemy; by healing the man he demonstrates the authority he claims (Mark 2:1–12). He then calls Levi from a tax booth and shares a meal with tax collectors and sinners, insisting that he has come to call sinners rather than the self-assured righteous (Mark 2:13–17). Questions about fasting prompt his bridegroom, cloth, and wineskin images (Mark 2:18–22). When disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath, he appeals to David's need and states that the Sabbath was made for humanity and that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:23–28). The chapter centers on Jesus' authority and conflict over forgiveness, social boundaries, and religious practice.

Mark 3.summary: In a synagogue Jesus heals a man with a withered hand despite observers watching for grounds to accuse him; he asks whether the Sabbath permits doing good or harm (Mark 3:1–6). Crowds gather from wide areas and Jesus heals many, while unclean spirits identify him (Mark 3:7–12). He appoints twelve to be with him, preach, and cast out demons (Mark 3:13–19). Relatives think he is out of his mind, and scribes from Jerusalem attribute his exorcisms to Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the image of a divided kingdom and a strong man bound, and warns against blaspheming the Holy Spirit in the context of their accusation (Mark 3:20–30). When his mother and brothers seek him, he identifies those who do God's will as his family (Mark 3:31–35). The chapter contrasts the growth of his mission with misunderstanding and resistance.

Mark 4.summary: From a boat Jesus teaches a large crowd beside the lake. The parable of the sower pictures varied responses to the word; he explains the parable privately to his followers and speaks about the revealing purpose of a lamp and the responsibility to hear (Mark 4:1–25). The growing seed and mustard seed depict God's kingdom developing in ways that may begin unnoticed yet become extensive (Mark 4:26–34). Afterward a storm threatens their boat while Jesus sleeps; he stills wind and water, asks about the disciples' fear and faith, and they wonder who he is (Mark 4:35–41). The chapter connects hearing the kingdom message with trusting Jesus amid danger.

Mark 5.summary: Across the lake in the region called Gerasenes, Jesus encounters a man living among tombs who describes his many unclean spirits as 'Legion.' Jesus expels them, and a herd of pigs rushes into the lake; the frightened residents ask Jesus to leave. He commissions the restored man to tell his household what the Lord has done (Mark 5:1–20). Returning across the lake, Jesus follows Jairus toward his dying daughter. On the way a woman suffering twelve years of bleeding touches his garment and is healed; Jesus addresses her as daughter and speaks of her faith (Mark 5:21–34). After messengers report Jairus's daughter dead, Jesus tells him not to fear, raises the girl, and orders care and discretion (Mark 5:35–43). The chapter portrays restoration from isolation, illness, and death.

Mark 6.summary: Jesus teaches in his hometown but meets disbelief from people familiar with his family (Mark 6:1–6). He sends the Twelve in pairs to preach repentance, heal, and travel dependently (Mark 6:7–13). Mark then recounts Herod Antipas's imprisonment and execution of John the Baptist after a banquet and a rash oath (Mark 6:14–29). After the apostles return, Jesus seeks rest but has compassion on the crowd, teaches them, and feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets remaining (Mark 6:30–44). He walks on the lake toward the disciples in a storm, and Mark remarks on their failure to understand the loaves (Mark 6:45–52). At Gennesaret people bring the sick, who seek to touch him and are healed (Mark 6:53–56). The chapter juxtaposes rejection, costly witness, provision, and difficult discipleship.

Mark 7.summary: Pharisees and scribes challenge disciples' eating with unwashed hands according to elder traditions. Jesus rebukes hypocrisy, cites Isaiah, and criticizes the way a tradition concerning gifts to God can evade care for parents (Mark 7:1–13). He teaches that what comes from the human heart defiles a person, listing destructive thoughts and conduct; Mark adds an explanatory comment about foods (Mark 7:14–23). In the region of Tyre a Syrophoenician woman asks Jesus to free her daughter; after an exchange using the image of children and dogs, he grants her request (Mark 7:24–30). In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man who struggles to speak, eliciting astonishment (Mark 7:31–37). The chapter addresses inward moral purity, the misuse of traditions, and faith expressed beyond Israel's usual boundaries.

Mark 8.summary: Jesus feeds about four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish, leaving seven baskets (Mark 8:1–10). Pharisees demand a sign; Jesus refuses, and later warns disciples about the yeast of the Pharisees and Herod, while they misunderstand his teaching as a concern about bread (Mark 8:11–21). In Bethsaida he restores a blind man's sight in stages (Mark 8:22–26). Near Caesarea Philippi, Peter identifies Jesus as the Messiah, but when Jesus predicts suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection, Peter objects and is sharply rebuked (Mark 8:27–33). Jesus then calls anyone following him to self-denial and taking up the cross, asking what it profits someone to gain the world but lose life (Mark 8:34–38). The chapter contrasts physical sight with incomplete understanding of the Messiah's suffering vocation.

Mark 9.summary: Jesus tells some followers they will see God's kingdom come with power (Mark 9:1). Six days later he is transfigured before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah appearing; a heavenly voice commands them to listen to him (Mark 9:2–13). Descending, he frees a boy whom the disciples could not help and teaches about prayer amid the father's anguished plea for help with unbelief (Mark 9:14–29). Jesus again predicts betrayal, death, and resurrection, but the disciples do not understand (Mark 9:30–32). After they argue about greatness, he teaches that the first must become servant of all and embraces a child (Mark 9:33–37). He corrects exclusionary attitudes toward a person expelling demons in his name and warns gravely against causing little ones to stumble, using forceful images of judgment and calling for peace (Mark 9:38–50).

Mark 10.summary: In Judea beyond the Jordan, Pharisees ask about divorce. Jesus contrasts Moses' concession with the creation ideal and later teaches privately against divorce and remarriage (Mark 10:1–12). He welcomes children when disciples turn them away (Mark 10:13–16). A wealthy man asks about eternal life; Jesus challenges him to sell his possessions and follow, leading to teaching about wealth's difficulty and God's ability to save (Mark 10:17–31). On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his death and resurrection again (Mark 10:32–34). James and John request high places of honor, but Jesus teaches that greatness requires service and says the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:35–45). Near Jericho he restores blind Bartimaeus, who then follows him on the road (Mark 10:46–52).

Mark 11.summary: Approaching Jerusalem, Jesus arranges for a colt and enters amid crowds spreading cloaks and branches and acclaiming the coming kingdom of David (Mark 11:1–11). The next day he curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree and enters the temple, driving out buyers and sellers and condemning the corruption of a house meant for prayer for all nations (Mark 11:12–19). The disciples later notice the fig tree withered; Jesus teaches trust in God, prayer, and forgiving others (Mark 11:20–25). When chief priests, scribes, and elders question his authority in the temple, he replies with a question about John's baptism that they decline to answer (Mark 11:27–33). The juxtaposition of fig tree and temple acts signals judgment on fruitless religious practice.

Mark 12.summary: Jesus tells a parable of tenant farmers who mistreat a landowner's servants and kill his beloved son; leaders realize it concerns them (Mark 12:1–12). Pharisees and Herodians ask about paying tax to Caesar; Jesus answers by distinguishing Caesar's claims from God's (Mark 12:13–17). Sadducees raise a resurrection puzzle, and Jesus disputes their understanding of Scripture and God's power (Mark 12:18–27). A scribe asks the chief commandment; Jesus joins love of God from Deuteronomy with love of neighbor from Leviticus (Mark 12:28–34). He then questions assumptions about David's son, warns against scribes who seek honor and exploit widows, and observes a poor widow placing two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:35–44). The chapter examines authority, faithful love, sincerity, and costly giving.

Mark 13.summary: Leaving the temple, Jesus predicts its destruction and answers Peter, James, John, and Andrew about coming upheaval (Mark 13:1–4). He warns against deceptive messianic claims, wars, earthquakes, persecution, and betrayal, urging endurance (Mark 13:5–13). He speaks of the 'abomination of desolation,' flight from Judea, severe distress, and misleading signs (Mark 13:14–23). Cosmic imagery accompanies the coming of the Son of Man and gathering of the elect (Mark 13:24–27). The fig tree illustrates attentive discernment, while Jesus insists that the day or hour is unknown and repeatedly calls disciples to remain awake (Mark 13:28–37). Interpretations differ on how the discourse relates to the Roman destruction of the temple in 70 CE and to future fulfillment; the chapter itself emphasizes vigilance rather than date setting.

Mark 14.summary: Chief priests and scribes plot against Jesus near Passover (Mark 14:1–2). In Bethany an unnamed woman anoints Jesus with costly perfume; he defends her act as preparation for his burial, while Judas later seeks to betray him (Mark 14:3–11). At the Passover meal Jesus foretells betrayal, shares bread and cup as his body and covenant blood, and predicts the disciples' scattering and Peter's denial (Mark 14:12–31). In Gethsemane he prays for the cup to pass yet submits to God's will, while the disciples sleep (Mark 14:32–42). Judas arrives with an armed crowd, Jesus is arrested, and followers flee (Mark 14:43–52). Before the high priest and council Jesus is accused and condemned after declaring his identity; Peter denies him three times and weeps (Mark 14:53–72). The chapter portrays devotion, betrayal, suffering, and failed loyalty.

Mark 15.summary: Early in the morning leaders hand Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate questions him, releases Barabbas after crowd pressure, and orders Jesus flogged and crucified (Mark 15:1–15). Soldiers mock him as king of the Jews and lead him out; Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross (Mark 15:16–21). Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two others, mocked by passersby and leaders. Darkness falls, and Jesus cries out with words from Psalm 22 before dying; the temple curtain tears, and a centurion calls him God's Son (Mark 15:22–39). Women followers watch from a distance (Mark 15:40–41). Joseph of Arimathea obtains his body and places it in a rock-cut tomb, while Mary Magdalene and Mary mother of Joses see where he is laid (Mark 15:42–47). The chapter presents Jesus' death as the stark climax of his ministry.

Mark 16.summary: After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome come with spices to anoint Jesus. They find the stone moved and a young man in white inside the tomb who announces that Jesus, the crucified one, has been raised and tells them to inform the disciples and Peter that he goes before them to Galilee (Mark 16:1–7). They flee trembling and astonished and, as Mark 16:8 states, initially say nothing because they are afraid. Many KJV and later manuscript traditions continue with verses 9–20: appearances to Mary Magdalene and others, a commission to preach, signs associated with believers, and Jesus' ascension (Mark 16:9–20). The two earliest surviving complete Greek manuscripts end at 16:8, and many textual scholars regard 9–20 as a later ending; its content is therefore presented here as part of the KJV textual tradition, not as unquestionably original to Mark. The chapter centers on the resurrection announcement and the varied textual witness to the book's conclusion.
